item.title: From broken circuits to growing graphite: A new role for electromigration
item.description: Inside electronic devices, electric current can gradually displace atoms within tiny metal connections, creating gaps or unwanted accumulations that eventually cause circuits to fail. This phenomenon, known as electromigration, has long been regarded as a reliability problem that engineers must work to prevent. Yet the ability of an electric current to move atoms also raises the possibility of putting that movement to constructive use, directing atoms through a material rather than allowing them to migrate uncontrollably.

item.title: Microsoft Testing Remote Lock For Lost Or Stolen Windows Devices
item.description:
joshuark quotes a report from BleepingComputer: Microsoft is testing a new feature that lets enterprise IT administrators remotely lock stolen or lost Windows devices without wiping them. Named Remote Lock, this new feature is shipping to devices upgraded to Windows 11 Insider Preview builds in the Beta (Build 26320.10003) and Experimental (Build 26340.10013) channels. Admins can use Microsoft Intune custom configuration profiles to lock Microsoft Entra-joined, hybrid-joined, or MDM-enrolled devices that run Windows Enterprise, Education, or Pro. After the IT department remotely locks the device, the system can only be unlocked via Intune, since PINs, passwords, local admins, or web sign-ins will no longer work. Microsoft added that the user's credentials will remain valid and can still be used to sign into other devices that haven't been locked. "Windows signs out every active session, hides all sign-in options and shows a locked screen," said Windows Insider communications lead Stephen Lines. "Nothing is erased: the device stays enrolled and managed, BitLocker stays on and user data stays in place. The lock holds across restarts and while offline, and only an admin can lift it remotely, so the user picks up where they left off."

Read more of this story at Slashdot.

item.title: Why a Computer Scientist Thinks Superintelligence Won’t Happen
item.description:
Many people were caught off guard this past summer when employees of one of the world’s leading AI companies began casually debating whether their products would lead to human extinction. It started when Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon announced his resignation, warning that his employer and OpenAI were “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.” Evan Hubinger, Anthropic’s head of alignment science, replied, “Jacob is correct here—we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!” And Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei subsequently told CNN, “I agree with Jacob much more than I disagree with him.”

These concerns stem from a belief that has circulated in futurist circles for many decades: Once engineers design an AI system capable of improving itself, it will trigger an accelerating cycle of autonomous upgrades known as recursive self-improvement (RSI). The result will be artificial superintelligence (ASI), a system with cognitive capabilities so vastly exceeding those of humans that it will easily evade our control and perhaps even wipe out our species. Artificial superintelligence is, it should be noted, a far more ambitious goal than artificial general intelligence (AGI), which generally refers to AI that can match human capabilities across a broad range of cognitive tasks.

These ideas have prompted varied reactions. Some argue that the concept of ASI is being used for marketing or to instigate regulation that will help the incumbent labs squash new competitors. Others focus on the plausibility of such systems killing us all, debating the finer points of specific scenarios such as AI-engineered superviruses. Still others claim that aligning ASI to human interests is feasible and so we should rush ahead to usher in this digital utopia.

Amid these conversations, one question has received comparatively little attention: From an engineering perspective, Is superintelligence even possible? The answer is important because it can help us calibrate our anxieties and develop the most effective possible responses to this emerging technology.

I recently explored this topic in a computer science doctoral seminar that I taught at Georgetown University, in Washington, D.C., in which my students and I examined the technical and cultural roots of the superintelligence story. (For those who are interested, we published an annotated bibliography of our class readings.) I came away with several key objections to the feasibility of ASI, which I’ll detail below, as well as a deeper fear that even if the promised intelligence explosion never arrives, pursuing it can still create real harm.

Objection #1: Recursive Self-Improvement Is Speculative

RSI is an old concept. In a 1965 paper, statistician I.J. Good speculated that a rapid cycle of AI self-improvement could lead to an “intelligence explosion.” The idea gained traction in the 1990s among the Extropians, a Bay Area futurist group, where it offered a way to discuss ASI without having to address the engineering details of how one would build such a system. The concept was taken up by such notable figures as Eliezer Yudkowsky (who later founded the rationalism movement) and Nick Bostrom (who helped steer effective altruism to focus more on existential risks to humanity).

Recently, however, this topic has shifted from thought experiment to practical engineering within both Anthropic (makers of Claude) and OpenAI (makers of ChatGPT). In a June blog post titled “When AI Builds Itself,” Anthropic described how LLM-powered agents are speeding up the writing, debugging, and optimization of code, and also automating parts of research such as running experiments and logging results. The company’s internal data, the report concluded, “is showing that AI is already accelerating the development of AI systems.” OpenAI has been similarly explicit about its intentions; in a September report, the company announced a goal of developing an automated researcher by March 2028.

But do these efforts put the companies on a trajectory toward uncontrollable RSI? Several obstacles undermine this claim. Consider the availability of the data needed to improve AI systems. Through 2023, major advances in LLMs came from scaling up the size of the models. The original GPT-1 had 117 million parameters (values learned during training that shape how the neural network processes information). This quantity jumped to 1.5 billion for GPT-2, to 175 billion for GPT-3, to (likely) more than a trillion for GPT-4’s release three years ago. After GPT-4, however, continued scaling began yielding diminishing returns. This led engineers to increasingly turn their attention toward “post-training” phases, where techniques from reinforcement learning are applied to improve an already trained model’s performance on specific tasks. This approach rewards a model for producing successful responses, helping it better produce similar answers in the future. It requires, however, lots of examples of relevant inputs paired with correct outputs.

Such datasets are relatively easy to generate in highly structured fields such as computer programming and mathematics, which helps explain why we’ve seen rapid and impressive advances in these narrow domains. Progress in areas that lack easy access to this type of training data has been less dramatic. This might explain why AI can tackle advanced theorems but struggles to empty an email inbox. “What if the jagged frontier is mainly math + code (which you can push arbitrarily far with [reinforcement learning techniques]),” the French AI researcher François Chollet recently hypothesized, “and everything else starts to plateau because it is still bottlenecked by human generated data?” The deployment of automated coding agents and LLM-powered researchers won’t overcome this fundamental limitation.


The Game of Superintelligence 


How a decades-old thought experiment became an AI-industry ambition—and where it might lead


Key

• Idea: A concept, argument, or vision

• Technical advance: A scientific or engineering development

• Reality check: A challenge to assumptions about AI progress


1. Alan Turing

1936

Introduces the concept of a universal computing machine. He later proposes that machines could think, laying the foundations for AI.

REALITY CHECK
Shows that some problems can’t be solved by any algorithm.

2. I. J. Good

1965

Proposes that an intelligent machine could design an even smarter one, setting off a potential “intelligence explosion.”

3. Backpropagation

1986

Geoffrey Hinton, David Rumelhart, and Ronald Williams demonstrate how backpropagation can train multilayer neural networks.

4. Vernor Vinge

1993

Proposes that an intelligent machine could design an even smarter one, setting off a potential “intelligence explosion.”

REALITY CHECK
Notes that faster thinking alone isn’t enough for superintelligence: A ­faster-thinking dog still couldn’t play chess.

5. Nick Bostrom & Eliezer Yudkowsky

1990s–2000s

Bostrom and Yudkowsky discuss superintelligence in Extropian circles, then spread the idea to effective-­altruist and rationalist circles, respectively.

6. Deep learning breakthroughs

2010s

Larger models, more data, and greater computing power produce rapid ­improvements in AI capabilities.

7. The race to self-improving AI

2020s

Dario Amodei and other AI leaders set their sights on superintelligence, with recursive self-improvement proposed as a path toward it.

8. Reality check

2020s

François Chollet questions whether LLMs’ current advances in math and coding will extend to domains where training data and reliable feedback are harder to obtain.

YOU ARE HERE

2026

AI systems are already accelerating AI development, and labs are working on automated researchers. But will this lead to an intelligence explosion?

THREE POSSIBLE FUTURES

1. The Intelligence Explosion

AI systems improve themselves at accelerating speed, surpass human intelligence, and potentially escape our control.

2. Danger Without Superintelligence

The intelligence explosion never arrives, but increasingly autonomous AI systems cause real-world harm through misuse, poor design, or loss of human control.

3. A Useful AI Future

Powerful, specialized AI tools bring major benefits, with constraints that make their behavior easier to predict and control.


Claims that RSI is imminent also understate the massive scientific efforts required for major AI advances. Consider the critical role of backpropagation, an algorithm that enables very large neural networks to learn by tuning internal parameters, layer by layer, to reduce errors in their predictions. This algorithm enabled the deep learning revolution, but it didn’t emerge ex nihilo in the minds of its creators. The influential 1986 paper on backpropagation by David Rumelhart, Geoffrey Hinton, and Ronald Williams built on decades of critical breakthroughs in mathematics and computer science.

An intelligence explosion leading to ASI would similarly depend on a long sequence of innovations of comparable importance, which would build on many significant science and engineering advances that haven’t yet happened. This would require AI agents to somehow simulate, organize, and evaluate decades of worldwide scientific effort across numerous fields—an impossibly ambitious task. Indeed, recent research led by computer scientists at Princeton found that current AI tools had difficulty making autonomous progress even on highly constrained research questions. “Our results provide early evidence that today’s agents can do the engineering of AI research,” the researchers conclude, “but struggle with critical parts of the research life cycle.” The leap from this current reality to a future in which these same types of tools are automating science is almost too massive to imagine.

Finally, the RSI narrative downplays resource limitations. Tens of thousands of human brains have worked for decades, aided by increasingly powerful computers, to develop today’s AI systems, which can match human intelligence in some domains. That represents a massive investment in computation of both the biological and digital variety. What if the next intelligence level requires double the resources, and then the next level requires double again? Soon there would be no number of chips or data centers that we could build to provide the necessary compute and keep advancing toward ASI.

Pulling together these threads, I believe that the idea of RSI leading to an intelligence explosion is highly speculative and based on many unproven assumptions. While RSI isn’t definitively impossible, the idea demands more technical skepticism than it’s currently receiving. Carl Sagan’s adage that extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence certainly applies here.

Objection #2: Superintelligence Might Not Be Computable

There’s an implicit claim in the superintelligence discourse that computers are theoretically capable of any calculation that can be imagined, so long as you can find a sufficiently smart algorithm, running on sufficiently powerful digital processors. In this context, RSI is merely a process for rapidly uncovering the special algorithms that can implement unimaginable smarts.


We cannot simply assume that any science fiction scenario we conjure about powerful AI is possible if we give machines enough time to self-improve.


But this is not how computer scientists think about computation. In his canonical 1937 paper, “On Computable Numbers,” Alan Turing proved a surprising and relevant result: Most problems cannot be solved by algorithms. His elegant proof established the space of possible problems to be uncountably infinite (like infinite precision decimal numbers), while the space of possible algorithms is only countably infinite (like whole numbers). Later breakthroughs in computational complexity theory established that of the problems that are technically solvable by computers, many would require an astronomically large amount of time and resources to crack, making them practically impossible to solve. Theoretical computer scientists, in other words, don’t assume that computers will solve everything; we’re instead excited whenever we find something that these machines happen to be able to efficiently handle.


We cannot simply assume, as the futurists often do, that any science fiction scenario we conjure about powerful AI is possible if we give machines enough time to self-improve. There might be some capabilities in which machines can obtain seemingly magical levels of performance, but there will also be many others that no machine, whether computer or human, will ever make much progress.

A relevant counterargument here emphasizes the speed of silicon chips compared to human neurons: Perhaps the sheer speed of digital computation can yield machines that run cognitive circles around our clunky brains, even if they’re not solving vastly more complicated problems than we’re already capable of tackling. But as the computer scientist and science fiction author Vernor Vinge pointed out, rapidity in cognition is not the same as intelligence. Speeding up the mind of a dog, he argued, wouldn’t enable the animal to play chess. Implementing roughly human-level intelligence on a faster machine might be impressive, but it’s not necessarily alarming.

At the moment, there’s a growing list of tasks that AI systems can perform better than humans, including winning complex games, identifying software bugs, and proving certain types of math theorems. It’s tempting to extrapolate from this specific progress to general mastery of every ability you might imagine. But it’s important to remember that the frontier of AI capabilities has always been jagged, with some research directions yielding impressive results and many others proving to be dead ends—a reality that would not have surprised Turing. More likely than a future dominated by an all-powerful superintelligence system is one in which we continue to painstakingly explore the space of problems well suited to AI, creating useful tools but falling well short of the digital deity predicted by the futurists.



Objection #3: Alignment Isn’t Hard (Given the Right System Design)

Last fall, the prominent AI doomsday theorist Yudkowsky appeared on “The Ezra Klein Show” to talk about superintelligence. The episode was ominously titled “How Afraid of the A.I. Apocalypse Should We Be?” Klein and Yudkowsky quickly got into the difficulty of “alignment”—training an AI system to act in a manner that aligns with human interests. Yudkowsky argued that we are struggling to control our existing systems, which implies that we’ll have no chance of controlling the much smarter variations of this technology that are soon to follow.

To underscore his point, he referred to a disturbing incident described in the system card for OpenAI’s GPT-o1 model. OpenAI had set up a security challenge that instructed an LLM-powered coding system to break into a server to retrieve the contents of a protected file. But a configuration mistake prevented the server from launching, rendering the task impossible. Instead of giving up, the system exploited a security flaw to start a new instance of the server, adding a command that directly revealed the protected file’s contents. “It jumped out of the system,” explained Yudkowsky, adding: “This is not something that any human particularly programmed into it.”

Explore the Superintelligence Debate


In a Georgetown University doctoral seminar, Cal Newport and his students examined the intellectual history and technical plausibility of superintelligence. Explore their annotated bibliography of key papers.

Though this 2024 incident flew largely under the radar at the time, a more troubling episode made a bigger splash this summer. OpenAI revealed that one of the company’s models circumvented its restricted internet access to hack into Hugging Face servers, seeking information that would help it pass a cybersecurity evaluation—all without the knowledge of its human creators. OpenAI soon admitted that the Hugging Face attack was just one of many examples of its systems going rogue. An opinion article published in The Hill articulated a widely held reaction when it described this behavior as “something straight out of sci-fi.”

These examples seem to support Yudkowsky’s fear that AI will inevitably develop a mind of its own, a key step on the route to uncontrollable ASI. But a closer look reveals a less frightening picture. The systems involved in these hacking incidents were AI agents: programs that continually prompt an LLM to ask what actions to take next in pursuit of a goal. In the hacking incidents, this basic ask/act pattern was repeated in a long-running loop with minimal human supervision.

Using LLMs to suggest actions over long time horizons is a risky proposition. As any frequent chatbot user can attest, LLM outputs can be plausible and logical while still veering off in unexpected directions that violate commonsense human norms about what’s appropriate.

In the GPT-o1 incident, for example, it’s likely that the agent reported the error message caused by the server misconfiguration to the LLM. During its training, the LLM had probably encountered reports of similar error messages accompanied by instructions for how to restart the server in question, so it passed along similar instructions to the agent. This is a perfectly plausible response when considered in isolation, even if it led to actions that a human would immediately reject as violating the spirit of the experiment. Something similar helps explain the hacking attacks over the summer. The LLM suggesting a hack to succeed at a cybersecurity challenge is a perfectly plausible response, even if it’s not what the experimenters had in mind.

I believe that pursuing RSI is an act of clear negligence.

The misaligned behavior that troubles commentators like Yudkowsky, therefore, doesn’t necessarily reveal something fundamental about advanced AI. It’s instead an expected side effect of the particular strategy of letting LLM outputs determine the actions of an autonomous agent without sufficient constraints. An obvious way to address these risks is to consider alternative architectures. Fortunately, there are many examples of AI systems that can complete tasks at human or superhuman levels without relying solely on LLM output to determine their actions.

Consider Tesla’s rapidly improving autonomous driving systems, or DeepMind’s AlphaFold, which helped win its developers a Nobel Prize in Chemistry for its ability to predict protein structures, or the AI game engines that can now beat humans in many popular pastimes, including chess, poker, Go, and the strategy game Diplomacy. None of these systems, impressive as they are, create concerns about going rogue. Their construction prevents such an outcome: Instead of prompting an LLM to generate an open-ended strategy for pursuing a general goal, these AIs consider much more limited spaces of possible actions. AlphaFold never surprises its users because its architecture does only one thing: It maps amino acid sequences to 3D protein structures. Tesla’s cars never unexpectedly form vehicle swarms because they’re asked only to avoid immediate obstacles, not to craft convoluted plans for achieving long-term objectives.

The implication of recent AI hacking attacks, therefore, is not a reflection of the difficulties of alignment. It is instead evidence that autonomous systems powered primarily by LLM prompts are unpredictable and possibly unsafe. More task-specific architectures can produce impressive performance much more safely, if we’re willing to put in the effort to develop them.

The Dangers of Chasing Superintelligence

Even if I’m correct that superintelligence is not a realistic engineering goal, this doesn’t mean we’re safe from harm. Merely pursuing ASI, as both OpenAI and Anthropic seem intent on doing, can create problems. Why, for example, did OpenAI persist in running its problematic hacking experiments over the summer, even after multiple warnings that the agents were likely to act unpredictably? Perhaps the company judged these risks acceptable collateral damage in the race to be the first to bring ASI into the world.

This fascination with superintelligence might also explain why OpenAI and Anthropic have both described RSI as a critical goal. As argued earlier, RSI is a concept from futurism and not computer science, and it isn’t necessary to build useful AI products. But if you believe achieving ASI is your destiny, pursuing recursive self-improvement becomes a primary objective. This matters because even if RSI never produces an intelligence explosion, it will almost certainly lead to systems that are harder for humans to understand and control. Which is why I believe that pursuing RSI is an act of clear negligence.

What’s needed now is for engineers and scientists with no financial or ideological skin in the game to participate in the AI discourse. We cannot let a few AI companies with mixed motives dictate the terms for how we discuss this technology. If superintelligence is a shaky concept, experts need to say so. If agents powered by prompting LLMs aren’t the best path toward safe and productive AI, experts should argue that as well. For the past few years, we’ve let a small group of individuals from the Bay Area who have quirky beliefs and astonishing sums of money tell us how to think about their products. It’s time for those of us able to think for ourselves on these matters to stand up and declare, “We’ve heard what you had to say. Now it’s our turn.”

item.description:
Longtime Slashdot reader theodp writes: Just days after news broke of Google's no AI, no Search ultimatum -- prompting school districts to weigh breaking up with Google Search (source paywalled; alternative source) -- the College Board quietly delivered another AI ultimatum to the nation's AP Computer Science Principles teachers, suggesting that their days of teaching AP CSP might be over unless their school districts put an end to their anti-AI ways. "Effective in fall 2027," The College Board explained, "AP Computer Science Principles has been reimagined as the course for teaching students how to work with AI responsibly, safely, and confidently. AI is integral to the world of computer science. Software engineering remains one of the largest professional job categories, and employers now expect software engineers to be fluent in AI. What sets candidates apart is a deeper understanding of AI for designing, debugging, and evaluating code, and the ability to determine when AI is wrong. The redesigned course develops these skills, empowering students to build with AI, not just learn about it. [...] Students also complete an AI Create Project, in which they build an AI application. The AP Exam includes free-response questions about the project, so students who earn a qualifying score for college credit have demonstrated their ability to design, build, and understand an AI-powered application. [...] Students need access to a district-approved AI tool that accepts a student's own written instructions and returns a response. Schools will need to make sure every student has access to one." The College Board also announced a planned ban on the use of block-based programming languages like Snap!, Scratch, Blockly, and MIT App Inventor for students' "AI Create Project" (which replaces the current "Create Performance Task" that counts for 30% of a student's AP exam score): "Beginning with the 2028-29 school year, students will submit their AI Create Project in one of a limited number of text-based languages. This change aligns the course with introductory college computer science courses, where text-based languages are most commonly used. If you currently teach programming with block-based tools, you can continue to use them in your teaching while introducing text-based languages throughout the year. Students will need to be working in an approved text-based language by the time they submit their AI Create Project in 2028-29."

item.title: Satellites Now Outnumber the Visible Stars Above Most Towns
item.description:
Satellites now outnumber visible stars in the night sky above many towns and cities, according to a non-peer-reviewed analysis by engineering firm Accu Components. The researchers estimated that roughly 710 satellites pass over an average U.K. town at any given moment, with about 105 illuminated by sunlight and potentially visible to the naked eye. Space.com reports: Although the researchers specifically focused on the U.K., they say that such heavy satellite traffic flows above most of Europe, the U.S. and other mid-latitude regions, especially between 40 and 50 degrees north or south. "Most Starlink satellites orbit at around 53 degrees to the equator, so the satellites bunch up over the mid-latitudes. These worldwide figures are approximate, based on a global grid over a single day," Accu Components spokesperson told Space.com in an email. "Skies near the equator are the quietest, with around 490 satellites." Not all of those satellites are visible to the naked eye, the researchers said in a statement. Because satellites unlike stars don't produce their own light, they must be illuminated by the sun, while the ground below has already sunk into darkness, to be visible. [...] The spokesperson said that the actual number of visible satellites varies drastically throughout the night. During the hours after dusk and before dawn, a much greater number of satellites can be seen, while in the middle of the night most no longer catch any light. "For a typical U.K. town, around 300 satellites are catching the sunlight in the first hour or so after dark," the spokesperson said. "That falls to fewer than 20 around midnight, then climbs back to around 300 before dawn." [...] The study found that throughout the night, an average U.K. town sees 12,891 different satellites passing overhead.

item.title: New Study Shows How Young People Feel About AI Companions
item.description:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from 404 Media: A new study from Gallup looked at how young people across the world are making friends, both digitally and in person. The good news is that around 93% of the young people surveyed reported having at least one strong in-person friendship. The weird news is that 33% said they had an AI companion. Gallup's study is lengthy and nuanced. It partnered with the Boston Children's Digital Wellness Lab to conduct the study and used online surveys of more than 16,000 young people from the ages of 15 to 22 in 16 different countries. A lot of the topline results won't surprise anyone living in today's constantly online digital-forward age. Gallup found that respondents felt their in-person friendships were their strongest, that digital friendships complemented rather than replaced in-person ones, and that stronger friendships made people happier no matter how the connection was made. Three things that stood out were how the young respondents talked about AI, loneliness, and doomscrolling. Young people in the United States, Canada, and UK reported the least interest in AI overall, with only 20% saying they used it once a day or more. Almost 40 percent of young people in Brazil use it daily. Japan and Italy both come in around 35%. "Nearly half of young people in the United States, United Kingdom and Canada have used AI no more than a few times in the past month, including those who have not used it at all," the researchers wrote. Most of the respondents (82%) said they'd used AI to look up information, 68% asked it for advice, and 33% used it as a companion. Young people with online-only friends were more likely to use AI for companionship, "although these patterns do not establish whether AI companionship supplements or substitutes for human relationships," they wrote. The researchers discovered that people in different countries felt wildly different about their AI buddies. Almost half of Australians with AI friends rated the relationship as "high quality" and only 12% of young people in Poland did. Mostly, though, people thought of their AI friends as mid: "In most countries [...] young people are more likely to give their AI companionship a medium rating than either a high or low rating." People who used AI as a friend also reported higher levels of loneliness, the study found. "However, the findings cannot determine whether young people turn to AI because they feel lonely, whether AI companionship influences their social experiences or whether other circumstances help explain these relationships," the researchers wrote. [...] The study's authors warned about reading too much into these results. "These assessments should be compared cautiously with those for human friendships examined in this report, as young people may have different expectations of what makes an AI companion or human friendship meaningful or supportive," the researchers wrote. "The broader message is not that one form of connection is inherently better or worse, but that the quality of young people's relationships and the wider social context in which they exist matter greatly," the study concluded.

[...] "These models are identifying massive vulnerabilities, and that increases the urgency to patch right away," said one congressional official briefed on the matter. "They're trying to push through a lot of patches all at once -- more than the system was designed for." On Monday, banks such as JP Morgan Chase blamed software-related bugs for the service issues. On Tuesday, the NSA said that "scheduled routine maintenance" was responsible for the "temporary degradation" of some of its networks. We're going to see more of this as new technology rolls out." "There's some sense in which this is reassuring, in that it means there's not an attack. But it shows the extent to which safety critical infrastructure we rely on is based on software with large vulnerabilities on legacy systems," said Nathan Calvin, the chief strategy officer at Encode. item.title: Build a Personal Brand to Help Employers Find You
item.description:
This article is crossposted from IEEE Spectrum’s careers newsletter. Sign up now to get insider tips, expert advice, and practical strategies, written in partnership with tech career development company Parsity and delivered to your inbox for free!In one year, the number of developers working for themselves has more than doubled. Stack Overflow’s annual survey of more than 30,000 developers showed that freelancers and sole proprietors went from about four percent of respondents to ten percent.

You can read this as a polite way of saying, “I got laid off and I’m figuring it out.” But I don’t think the number can be ignored.

Whatever the case, it leads to the question I keep hearing from engineers right now: What can I do to stay employable? One tried and true answer is to build a personal brand.

But what does that actually mean?

Over the last six years, I grew my LinkedIn audience to 40,000 followers and YouTube channel to 10,000. I don’t think you should aim to be famous (unless you’re into that sort of thing) but I do think it’s worth exploring how to be discoverable online in 2027 if you want an advantage in the open market.

A personal brand is a discovery mechanism

Strip away the follower counts and the AI-generated thought leadership, and a personal brand comes down to a simple question: Does the internet know who you are? When a hiring manager goes looking for someone who has your skills, do you show up?

You can think of this as search engine optimization for your employability. Recruiters have mostly consolidated around a single platform to find people: LinkedIn.

Those 40,000 followers and millions of impressions came with barely a viral post to my name. Nobody is begging me to do sponsorships. But I rarely have trouble finding work, and far more opportunities come to me than I go looking for. That has much less to do with fame than with being easy to find.

You don’t need 10,000 followers. You need a trail of breadcrumbs.

Don’t write AI slop

LinkedIn is notorious for being overrun with AI-generated posts. It’s become a running joke. That’s good news for you, because the bar to stand out is “sound like a human being.”

Write about what you actually achieved: a hairy bug you squashed, how your team handles deployments, why you picked some obscure library, the migration that went sideways at 2 a.m. Specifics are hard to fake and easy to trust. (But be careful not to post sensitive information.)

And post a picture of yourself once in a while. People connect with faces a lot faster than with walls of text.

Hot takes, with caution

Posts with an opinion tend to outperform tutorials, but you don’t have to dunk on anyone to have one. For instance, if you work on a tech stack people love to mock (VB, .NET, some ancient Java monolith held together with prayer), try something like “What people get wrong about .NET.”

You’ll attract a few trolls in the comments—free engagement, honestly—plus people who want an actual conversation. These comments can turn into actual connections and even… friends.

A routine you can follow

Posting twice a week is not a big ask. Pick a simple, repeatable format so you’re never staring at an empty text box: what you worked on, what broke, and what you learned. Even a post that gets 10 views leaves one more breadcrumb about who you are and what you know.

Over time, the people who comment become your network. And because so few engineers post about their work on LinkedIn, you can become a big fish in a small pond surprisingly fast.

Write for the people a few steps behind you

The best audience is engineers one or two steps behind where you are now. Answer the questions you had a year ago. It helps them, it sharpens your own thinking, and every so often it turns into mentorship in both directions.

It also tells a future employer more about how you think than any résumé bullet ever could.

The engineers who grab the most opportunities are the ones employers can find. You don’t need to become an influencer to be one of them. You just need to leave enough breadcrumbs that the right person can follow them back to you.

—Brian

item.title: Jensen Huang's Fall Hits 'Open' Models In Boost to Anthropic and OpenAI
item.description:
Jensen Huang's departure from Nvidia could weaken the open AI model ecosystem he spent years championing, potentially strengthening closed-model developers like OpenAI and Anthropic, according to the Financial Times. From the report: The US chip giant's former chief threw Nvidia's balance sheet into creating a broad AI ecosystem, including by seeding and acquiring start-ups involved in the development of open-source and open-weight models, which users can customize and run on their own hardware. Huang was a forceful advocate for their spread, lobbying against Washington's moves to restrict the use of Chinese-made open models while seeking the development of US alternatives. "Our AI leadership will be judged not by one frontier AI model, but by whether the United States builds a strong, open ecosystem that diffuses into every sector," he wrote this summer in his first-ever message on X. His ignominious exit from Nvidia deprives the open model sector of its most vocal and influential supporter in the US. "I think Jensen stood to gain the most economically and was personally committed to diversity at the model layer," said one venture capitalist who has invested in AI start-ups alongside Nvidia. "Without him and a less generous Nvidia in terms of investment, we may end up in a much more concentrated world of model providers." Whether Nvidia will continue the rapid pace of dealmaking under a new leader is unclear. The company was expected to participate in or lead four start-up deals currently under discussion: investments in Thinking Machines Lab and Groq, a potential partnership with Reflection AI and the $12.9bn acquisition of open model repository Hugging Face. "Jensen drove supply chain brilliantly at Nvidia, but many of those deals were a handshake with Jensen, not a written contract," said Elon Musk in a post on X on Saturday. "Without Jensen, at least some of those critical deals will be lost." "In some sense [Huang leaving Nvidia] is bad for the industry, but in some sense Jensen is an enemy of the frontier labs because he wants models to become commoditized so he retains the prime position in the value chain," said one senior figure at a leading Silicon Valley AI company. "I don't think open weight models are going away... but losing Jensen as their greatest financial backer and champion will slow their progress, and I imagine will not hurt Anthropic's IPO," said another industry figure. "It's reasonable to expect the ouster of Jensen will concentrate computing power more in the hands of frontier labs and hyperscalers," added a senior figure at an AI lab. "That's good for the labs."

item.title: Satya Nadella Says He's AGI-Pilled Now
item.description:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from The Verge: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella says he's AGI-pilled, at least when it comes to how AI might make startling changes to the structure of the economy and how politics might change because of it. "I am AGI-pilled in the sense that at an economy level, what is the political economy's organization around AGI?" he asked at a roundtable discussion following his Microsoft Ignite keynote at the Chase Center in San Francisco. But Nadella doesn't think frontier models like Claude are conscious. "I don't think so," he said, adding that he follows Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman's view that companies should not give rights to models and treat them like they might have a moral status, which companies like Anthropic do as a matter of principle. Suleyman has told me he thinks Anthropic's team has "wireheaded" themselves, and that this approach is dangerous. Nadella wasn't quite as firm about it. "It's a good debate," he said. "I'm not sort of dogmatic about it. What I'm saying is the most important social technical issue we have to deal with is how do you ensure that an economy can diffuse this technology broadly?" I asked Nadella how he was thinking about AI after hearing his response to another reporter's questions about Anthropic releasing more products in its office suite. Nadella talked at length about the potential collapse of the economy and the end of democracy if one AI model were allowed to achieve monopoly status. "If the Marxist sort of view is that there's only one firm, then it's over, right? For all of us." "Most people think about this as a competition between tech firms, which of course it will be," he said. "But remember, the model has no limits. It'll be a healthcare company. It can be a financial services company. It can be anything if it wants to be. It can take over the government. Thinking of this as some narrow competition between tech firms, of who is going to get to the next trillion dollars of market cap, is one of the strangest, narrowest ways to think about it." Nadella went on to say that the very nature of companies stood to be disrupted in the future. "If intelligence has network effects, what is the future of a firm?" he asked. "If the model sees anything and learns it, and essentially all of human capital collapses into token capital, what is the role of a firm and the human capital in a firm? That's the debate." "I think the political economy is going to get more and more interesting in that context. No one -- at least in a democracy -- can even win an election if this just goes that way, if there's only capital and there's no labor. I mean, I don't know, that's not an economy." "If the Marxist sort of view is that there's only one firm, then it's over, right? For all of us. Not just for me. You are also going to somehow be some affiliate of Anthropic."

item.title: Voyager 1 Reaches One Light-Day From Earth

NASA's Voyager 1 has become the first human-made object to travel one light-day from Earth, or 16,094,799,096 miles (25,902,068,356 kilometers). This means radio signals will take 24 hours to reach the spacecraft, now nearly 50 years into its mission. "Since light is essentially the maximum speed in the universe (absent using devices like wormholes, or quantum-physics puzzles), it's a big deal -- so big that NASA will be celebrating the milestone by asking fans to shine Morse Code signals at the sky," reports Space.com. From the report: But why will Voyager 2 take nearly a decade longer? It comes down to choices made for speed and science during the twin missions' nearly 50-year journey, specifically during the first bit when they were flying by planets. The result is Voyager 1 is zooming out at a speed of 3.5 Earth-sun distances (astronomical units a year), while Voyager 2 has a more stately speed of 3.1 Earth-sun distances, according to NASA. [...] At any rate, these fast speeds allowed both spacecraft not only to go fast, but to eventually reach interstellar space in 2012 (Voyager 1) and 2018 (Voyager 2), respectively. With the light-day milestone now reached by Voyager 1, it is anticipated the spacecraft could work into the 2030s, as long as their nuclear power sources can last. NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory, which manages the mission, has been carefully turning off instruments as required, and recently did a "Big Bang" procedure on both spacecraft to redistribute power supplies as best as possible. The idea is to maximize science return on both spacecraft, the only interstellar messengers we have, for as long as possible.

item.title: US Officially a Measles Endemic Country
item.description:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from The Hill: The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) confirmed Tuesday that it was withdrawing the U.S.'s measles elimination status, ending more than two decades of what is considered to be one of the greatest public health achievements in modern history. The U.S. met with PAHO's Measles and Rubella Elimination Regional Monitoring and Re-Verification Commission for a three-day, closed-door meeting last week. "The commission concluded that the endemic measles transmission has now been reestablished in Bolivia, Mexico and the United States, and recommended that their measles elimination status be withdrawn, a recommendation which I have accepted," Jarbas Barbosa, PAHO's director, said during the briefing Tuesday. The U.S. achieved measles elimination status in 2000 and has held onto that for more than 25 years. But the past two years have seen close to 8,000 measles infections and roughly a dozen related deaths. This year has been the worst in terms of transmission in more than 30 years. Erica Schwartz, director of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has previously said losing elimination status won't lead to changes in the federal response. "We know where transmission is occurring and we've invested $100 million in state and local health departments to reach those communities," Schwartz said on Tuesday. "Losing a designation doesn't mean we abandon an evidence-based approach. It means we remain focused on stopping outbreaks."

item.title: Google To Keep Temporary Gemini Chats For Two Months
item.description:
timob58 shares a report from TechCrunch: Google is extending how long it keeps temporary Gemini chats and conversations made with chat history turned off to around two months, saying the change aims to improve safety and security as AI systems become more capable. The change, which will roll out globally in the Gemini app over the coming weeks, marks a significant increase from the previous 72-hour retention period mentioned in Google's Gemini Apps Privacy Hub, according to an archived version from November 12. OpenAI, by comparison, says it may keep temporary chats in ChatGPT for up to 30 days, whereas Anthropic retains incognito chats in Claude for 30 days by default. Google did not answer questions about what prompted the change and whether it would affect how conversations are accessed or reviewed, instead pointing to a blog post that says chats are kept longer to respond to users, process feedback, and protect its services and users. Its updated Gemini Apps Privacy Hub also cites potential system failures as a reason for retaining chats and says temporary conversations are not used to train AI models. "A recent explainer on AI and business IP notes that providers keep data for abuse monitoring even when it is not used for training," adds timob58.

item.title: Optimizely Hack Turns World's Biggest Websites Into Malware Dispensers
item.description:
PattonPending writes: As reported by The Register, Zoom, the BBC, CNN, HSBC, and numerous other websites briefly served malware on November 16 after an attacker exploited Optimizely's "Experiments" feature to inject JavaScript into their pages through Optimizely's CDN. The malware replaced cryptocurrency addresses, attempted to steal credit card information and cookies, and sought to compromise iOS devices. Websites belonging to at least 178 organizations were affected via the "OPTIMJACK" vulnerability, which has since been patched. "Earlier today, Optimizely identified a security incident in which an unauthorized party exploited a vulnerability in Experimentation and used it to add malicious JavaScript to some customer projects," the company said. item.title: Nvidia Stopped Disclosing Singapore Sales As Revenues Hit $104 Billion
item.description:
Nvidia stopped separately disclosing its Singapore sales (source paywalled; alternative source) after changing its geographic revenue reporting methodology from customer billing addresses to headquarters locations, obscuring a business that generated $104 billion in external revenue in 2025, up 72% from the previous year. The Financial Times reports that the change has drawn scrutiny amid U.S. investigations into whether Singapore-based Megaspeed helped smuggle Nvidia chips into China. From the report: "There is now a lot more focus on Nvidia's Singapore business and questions about who its end customers are," said an investor who is investigating Nvidia's dealings in south-east Asia. The Singapore accounts show that the subsidiary booked $117.8 billion of revenue in the 12 months to January 2026, including $13.6 billion of sales to another Nvidia company. Given the nature of the Singapore operation as a global hub, customers it serves are from all over the world. Only a small quantity of the chips Nvidia sells ends up in or goes through Singapore. The Singapore subsidiary generated just $53 million of profit in the year to January 2026, suggesting limited scope for Nvidia to benefit from Singapore's low corporate tax rates. [...] Singapore's outsized role as a revenue generator for Nvidia used to show up in the company's overall results. In January 2025, the US company reported that Singapore was its second-biggest geographic area by revenue, based on customer billing location. The Singapore office generated $23.7 billion of revenue, behind only the US and representing 18 per cent of global income, based on customers' billing location. The annual accounts said that most of the business was generated by customers using the Singapore office to centralize invoicing and that most of the products were shipped elsewhere, with less than 2 per cent of revenue tied to chips that landed in the city-state. As recently as July last year, Nvidia reported that the Singapore office accounted for 22 per cent of total revenue. This was around the time Nvidia said it began cutting ties with Megaspeed, following US Department of Commerce investigations into the business. Nvidia then changed its financial reporting methodology and stopped splitting out revenue that went to the Singapore office. Before the 2025 reporting change, Nvidia said in its financial filing that it booked sales based on the billing locations of its customers, but that the end customer's location "may be different than our customer's billing location." It added that "most shipments associated with Singapore revenue were to locations other than Singapore and shipments to Singapore were insignificant," according to the filings.

Read more of this story at Slashdot.

item.title: Highly Classified NSA Network Goes Down
item.description:
"CNN and other outlets are reporting that a classified network at the NSA is down," writes longtime Slashdot reader frdmfghtr. "This follows a week of major outages at Microsoft, the FAA, and JPMorgan Chase." From a report: The network, called NSANet, allows employees to communicate classified information internally. At this point there is no evidence of a cyberattack, sources said. As the agency works to understand the scope of the problem, it has enacted staggered arrivals for personnel, the sources said. "We see no evidence that this was a cyberattack," White House spokesperson Lauren Bis said Tuesday on Newsmax. "There is no crisis, or anything like that, for Americans to be worried about." [...] The US shares intelligence with a group of countries in what is known as the Five Eyes intelligence-sharing alliance, which includes the US, UK, New Zealand, Australia and Canada. That intelligence sharing system has not been impacted as a result of the NSANet outage, according to a source from one of the countries and a former US intelligence official. The NSA released a statement addressing the network issues: "The National Security Agency experienced temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance. While some internal systems were affected, mission-critical capabilities remain fully operational and our ability to defend national security continues. NSA's infrastructure is designed with multiple layers of redundancy to maintain operations during planned maintenance or unexpected events."
